samples.title: Differentiable Vector Quantization for Rate-Distortion Optimization of Generative Image Compression

core_query.question: Extreme image compression faces a fundamental tension between reducing the transmitted information to an extremely low bitrate and preserving high reconstruction quality. Most learned perceptual compression methods build on the variational image compression framework, where analysis transforms, scalar quantization, entropy coding, and synthesis transforms are optimized jointly under a rate-distortion objective, while generative priors such as GANs or diffusion models are typically incorporated without fundamentally changing this formulation. At very low bitrates, however, pointwise scalar quantization may be inefficient in preserving structured feature information, which has motivated vector-quantized approaches that transmit compact discrete indices. Although such representations can be effective, their reconstruction objectives and subsequent entropy coding are often optimized separately rather than being jointly shaped by rate and distortion. This separation raises the possibility that representations learned only for reconstruction may not necessarily be easy to predict or encode, while the similarity between autoregressive token prediction in generative models and entropy modeling in compression suggests a deeper connection between the two problems. Can vector-quantized representations for extreme image compression be jointly shaped by both reconstruction quality and coding rate by exploiting the common probabilistic structure underlying autoregressive generation and entropy coding?

key_paper.title: Unifying Generation and Compression: Ultra-low bitrate Image Coding Via Multi-stage Transformer
key_paper.rationale: This work made an important connection between autoregressive generation and entropy coding: both require modeling the probability distribution of discrete tokens, and the same learned prior can therefore be used both to estimate probabilities for entropy coding and to generate missing image tokens. The idea I brought from this paper was that an autoregressive model should not be viewed only as a generative prior attached to a compression system. Its predicted token probabilities are also directly related to the number of bits required to encode those tokens. This suggested that autoregressive probability modeling could provide the rate signal needed to optimize a VQ representation itself, potentially bringing VQ-based compression closer to the joint rate-distortion optimization used in conventional learned compression. I expected this connection to be useful because the paper explicitly demonstrated the mathematical relationship between likelihood modeling and entropy estimation, and experimentally showed that applying entropy estimation to the same VQ codec improved its rate-distortion performance over the VQ-Kmeans baseline. These observations provided direct evidence that better probabilistic modeling of VQ indices translates into actual bitrate savings, motivating me to investigate whether the representation and the probabilistic model could be optimized together rather than in separate stages.

thread.question: Traditional learned image compression relies on scalar quantization with differentiable approximations to allow gradients from the rate penalty to update the encoder. Vector quantization provides structural advantages over scalar quantization but relies on discrete assignments that block these continuous gradients. How can the coding rate of discrete vector-quantized representations be modeled and incorporated into end-to-end rate-distortion optimization?
thread.criterion: End-to-End Optimized Image Compression (2017) established the foundation of end-to-end learned image compression by formulating compression as a rate-distortion optimization problem. It demonstrated that the encoder, decoder, and entropy model can be jointly optimized, allowing the rate term to directly influence the learned representation rather than treating compression as a separate coding stage. This principle provided the fundamental insight behind our investigation into how discrete representations could be optimized jointly with their coding efficiency. Variational Image Compression with a Scale Hyperprior (2018) further developed the end-to-end learned compression framework by introducing a learned scale hyperprior for more accurate entropy modeling. Beyond improving rate estimation, it reinforced the importance of jointly optimizing representation learning and entropy modeling under a rate-distortion objective. This insight motivated our exploration of whether vector-quantized representations could also benefit from a similar optimization principle, where coding efficiency contributes to shaping the learned discrete representation.

samples.title: MesaTask: Towards Task-Driven Tabletop Scene Generation via 3D Spatial Reasoning

core_query.question: Tabletop scene generation is fundamentally a structured layout generation problem, where a scene is defined not only by its constituent objects but also by their semantic attributes and spatial organization. However, a high-level manipulation instruction typically specifies only the desired task outcome, leaving the required objects, their interrelations, and their concrete geometric arrangements largely unspecified. Translating such an instruction into a complete scene therefore requires reasoning from task intent to a structured layout rather than merely retrieving relevant objects or satisfying isolated spatial constraints. Moreover, physically plausible tabletop arrangements must reflect realistic patterns of object co-occurrence, support, stacking, and containment that are difficult to fully prescribe with handcrafted rules alone. How can the implicit object composition and spatial organization required by a high-level robotic manipulation task be inferred to generate a realistic, physically plausible, and executable 3D tabletop scene?

key_paper.title: Holodeck: Language Guided Generation of 3D Embodied AI Environments
key_paper.rationale: Holodeck introduced a fully automated and modular workflow that converts a language prompt into an interactive 3D environment by using GPT-4 to infer scene content and spatial constraints, retrieving matching 3D assets, and optimizing object placements to satisfy those constraints. I adopted its key factorization between semantic scene planning and geometric instantiation: first determine what objects and relationships a scene should contain, and then realize that specification using retrieved assets. I extended this factorization to dense tabletop manipulation scenes and treated the metric layout itself as a learnable structured output, rather than leaving its realization entirely to a prompt-driven constraint optimizer. I expected the factorized representation and retrieval strategy to transfer because Holodeck's large-scale human evaluation favored its scenes over procedural baselines, and its generated environments were sufficiently functional for training embodied navigation agents, demonstrating that LLM-derived scene specifications can be instantiated as useful interactive environments.

thread.question: Large language models possess strong semantic priors that can be harnessed to translate high-level text prompts into structural arrangements of 3D objects in simulated environments. How can we design a structured reasoning process that allows a language model to infer necessary objects and final 3D bounding box layouts directly from abstract task instructions?
thread.criterion: These methods all utilize an LLM to generate scenarios based on instructions, including training and training-free methods.

samples.title: CAR-bench: Evaluating the Consistency and Limit-Awareness of LLM Agents under Real-World Uncertainty

core_query.question: Existing benchmarks for Large Language Model agents primarily focus on idealized task completion by assuming task solvability and providing complete information and full tool coverage upfront. While recent advancements have introduced dynamic multi-turn interactions and policy constraints to better mimic real-world operations, they still predominantly evaluate an agent's ability to successfully execute satisfiable tasks. In real user-facing settings, however, agents must operate under uncertainty, where requests may be ambiguous, information may be insufficient, or required capabilities may be unavailable, making reliable behavior depend not only on successful execution but also on recognizing when to clarify, refrain from acting, or proceed safely. A comprehensive evaluation should therefore assess whether agents consistently calibrate their behavior to the request, available information, capabilities, and applicable policies across both straightforward and uncertain situations. How can we systematically evaluate whether multi-turn, policy-guided agents exhibit consistent and calibrated action under real-world uncertainty, including when to act, when to seek clarification, and when not to act?

key_paper.title: $\tau$-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
key_paper.rationale: tau-bench established a realistic evaluation environment for agents operating in industry applications. Its key contribution was to identify three requirements for reliable real-world agents: (1) dynamic interaction with both users and programmatic APIs, (2) adherence to domain-specific rules and policies, and (3) consistency and robustness across repeated trials. In doing so, tau-bench moved agent evaluation beyond isolated tool-use tasks toward interactive, policy-constrained environments. The new idea I derived from this was to evaluate calibrated action. In tau-bench, tasks are generally constructed such that a correct solution exists and the information needed to reach it can be obtained through interaction. In real deployments, however, agents also encounter requests that exceed their capabilities or are underspecified in ways that make immediate action unsafe or inappropriate. I therefore extended the evaluation setting with unsatisfiable requests and ambiguous requests, requiring the agent to recognize when it should not act, when it should ask for clarification, and when execution is actually justified. I additionally transferred this evaluation paradigm to a domain in which I was able to personally incorporate detailed real-world constraints and expert knowledge. I expected this idea to work because tau-bench already showed that reliable real-world agents must adapt their behavior to interaction context and domain constraints rather than simply maximize task completion. Its results also demonstrated substantial failures in policy adherence and consistency even when tasks were solvable. This suggested that evaluating only whether an agent can successfully complete a feasible task leaves an important part of reliability unmeasured. Extending the benchmark to situations in which the correct behavior may be to clarify or refuse therefore provides a more complete test of whether an agent can calibrate its actions to its capabilities, the available information, and the constraints of the environment.

thread.question: Prior research investigates the tendency of language models to hallucinate plausible completions instead of admitting uncertainty and explores meta-reasoning strategies for active information gathering. How can we systematically evaluate an agent's ability to recognize its own limitations, resolve underspecified instructions, and gather necessary information before prematurely taking action?
thread.criterion: The positive papers are findings establishing that LLMs hallucinate, are missing self-awareness and disambiguation capability, and exploring why. The negative papers are frameworks around the model to improve as this can be benchmarked in the end with our established method but are not framing the research question and underlying problem.

samples.title: Spurious Rewards: Rethinking Training Signals in RLVR

core_query.question: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has proven highly effective at improving mathematical reasoning in large language models. Recent studies suggest that these techniques might not be teaching models novel reasoning skills but are instead eliciting latent capabilities acquired during pretraining. We wanted to explore unsupervised reinforcement learning methods. There have been methods showing that using a majority-voted answer as the ground-truth labels can also help improve the model performance. Therefore, we wondered if we can use that to help improve model performance, and if so, how much noise in the majority-voted labels can it tolerate.

key_paper.title: Self-Consistency Preference Optimization
key_paper.rationale: This paper performed RL training with majority-voted answers as the training labels and showed that such weak supervision can result in performance similar to that of ground-truth labels. There had not been a study showing how weak these signals could become while still providing meaningful training signals. We therefore tried progressively weaker signals in RL to see how it would work. We expected to observe a spectrum that would reveal the minimum signal needed for RL. The results were model-dependent, and for some models even random rewards could work, which led us to an analysis paper. Other papers on RL for reasoning do not consider using weak training signals derived from training-data annotations and thus did not provide useful guidance for addressing this question.

thread.question: Recent studies suggest that reinforcement learning for alignment primarily surfaces latent capabilities acquired during pretraining. How do the pre-existing reasoning strategies encoded in different base models influence their ability to improve reasoning performance during reinforcement learning post-training?
thread.criterion: The selected papers partially contributed to the intuition that RL is eliciting pre-existing behaviors, while we were not aware of the negative ones when coming up with this intuition or the topic is unrelated to this question.

samples.title: Adaptive Defense against Harmful Fine-Tuning for Large Language Models via Bayesian Data Scheduler

core_query.question: Fine-tuning-as-a-service allows users to adapt foundation models to specific tasks, but it also introduces a severe vulnerability known as harmful fine-tuning. Malicious users can inject a small fraction of harmful examples into their uploaded datasets to compromise the model's safety alignment established during pre-training. Existing defenses generally seek to establish robustness before fine-tuning by simulating attacks, yet this strategy is fundamentally constrained by the difficulty of extending attack simulations beyond bounded threat models and by its limited adaptability to varying attack settings. How can LLMs be protected against harmful fine-tuning under unknown and varying attack conditions without relying on attack simulation, while preserving their ability to learn from benign fine-tuning data?

key_paper.title: Safety-Aware Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models
key_paper.rationale: Safety-Aware Fine-Tuning (SAFT) introduced a data-centric defense that automatically identifies and removes potentially harmful examples before fine-tuning. Specifically, it constructs a harmfulness-related subspace from the model's internal representations, scores each example according to its projection onto that subspace, and uses a manually selected threshold to divide the fine-tuning dataset into retained and removed subsets. This work directly inspired our view that harmful fine-tuning should be addressed at the level of individual data examples because different examples can have substantially different effects on model safety. In our work, we extended this idea by replacing deterministic scoring and hard filtering with Bayesian inference: we model each example's safety attribute as a latent variable, infer its posterior distribution conditioned on the encountered fine-tuning and alignment datasets, and continuously weight its contribution during optimization rather than removing it outright. We expected this extension to work because SAFT showed that targeted filtering consistently reduced harmfulness across models and contamination ratios, while randomly removing the same number of examples was substantially less effective and preserving the selected data maintained helpfulness. Its additional finding that even some examples labeled as benign could adversely affect safety further suggested that fixed semantic labels or hard decisions may be insufficient, motivating our probabilistic and adaptive treatment of sample-level safety.

thread.question: Prior work has shown that stochastic gradient Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods enable scalable Bayesian inference for complex models by introducing controlled noise into gradient updates. In the context of learning from potentially untrusted data, robust training often requires estimating the unobserved reliability of each individual data point. How can we leverage scalable Bayesian sampling techniques to efficiently infer the posterior distributions of data-specific weights during model training?
thread.criterion: The positive papers provide the foundational ideas of SGLD and Bayesian data selection used in our work. We only rely on these basic principles and do not involve the more advanced extensions or improvements to SGLD studied in the remaining papers.

samples.title: Hi Robot: Open-Ended Instruction Following with Hierarchical Vision-Language-Action Models

core_query.question: Robots working in human-centric settings receive language that is far messier than the atomic commands studied in language-conditioned imitation learning. A line of work trains policies to map instructions such as "pick up the coke can" to actions and generalizes well within that regime, but real requests carry constraints, preferences, and mid-execution corrections ("that's not trash," "I'm allergic to pickles") whose meaning depends on what the robot is currently seeing and doing. A separate line of work uses LLMs and VLMs off the shelf to decompose long-horizon tasks over predefined or hand-designed skills. These systems parse richer language but inherit the limited dexterity of their skill libraries and rarely react to a user who interrupts mid-task. Both lines leave a gap between the semantics a system can interpret and the physical behavior it can actually produce, and it is not obvious whether that gap is best closed by making language interpretation more capable or by making dexterous learned policies more promptable. How can a robot with dexterous, learned manipulation skills interpret open-ended prompts and real-time human feedback, grounded in its own observations, and act on them while the task is underway?

key_paper.title: Yell At Your Robot: Improving On-the-Fly from Language Corrections
key_paper.rationale: YAY Robot showed that a two-level architecture, a high-level policy emitting short language commands, and a low-level language-conditioned policy executing them, lets a human intervene mid-episode by simply speaking. Corrections like "go lower" or "move to the left" are injected into the language channel between the layers, take effect immediately during a long-horizon bimanual task, and can subsequently be distilled back into the high-level policy to improve it. The key move was treating language not as a task specification given once at episode start, but as a live control interface that stays open while the robot acts. The idea I carried forward is that the interface between deliberative reasoning and reactive control should be natural language, and that this interface remains writable at execution time. That is the structural commitment underlying my work: whatever produces high-level commands can be swapped or made far more capable without touching the low-level policy, because the contract between them is just a short atomic instruction. YAY Robot's limitation is also what defined my question. Its high-level policy is trained on a single task prompt and on the specific correction phrases its human operators happened to utter, so the space of things a user can say is bounded by what appeared in the annotation set. Inheriting the interface but replacing the bottleneck became the direction. YAY Robot already provided the empirical evidence for the hard part: it demonstrated that a low-level policy trained on segmented skill labels genuinely responds to language issued mid-rollout, and that human corrections measurably raised success on a contact-rich long-horizon task. So the mechanism of real-time language steering was not speculative. It had been shown to move policy behavior on real hardware. What remained untested was whether the high-level end could be made open-ended rather than closed-vocabulary, which is a question about language coverage rather than about whether the control channel functions at all.

thread.question: A line of work already lets users correct a robot while it acts. Some approaches edit trajectories from verbal feedback, others train recovery behaviors from simulator-constructed perturbations, and others route spoken corrections through a language channel between a high-level and a low-level policy. Each demonstrates that mid-execution language can redirect behavior, but each is bounded: by a single task prompt, by the specific correction phrases human annotators happened to produce, or by feedback that never depends on what the robot is currently seeing. Utterances like "that's not trash" or "leave it alone" are unresolvable from text alone. They refer to whatever is in the gripper right now. What determines the range of corrections such a system can absorb, and can a robot ground feedback in its live observations while also handling phrasings and situations that never appeared in its interaction data?
thread.criterion: Positive papers each contribute a mechanism for a human to redirect a robot mid-execution with language grounded in the current scene, which is exactly what bounds the range of absorbable corrections. Negative papers contribute modality binding, cross-session adaptation, self-generated correction signals, reward synthesis, and in-context control loops, none of which turn on a human grounding feedback in what the robot is doing right now.

samples.title: Meta-Harness: End-to-End Optimization of Model Harnesses

core_query.question: The performance of large language model systems depends heavily on the surrounding harness. While recent work attempts to automate text optimization, these existing methods compress feedback into scalar scores or short summaries. This compression discards the long-horizon diagnostic information necessary for harness optimization. How can we fully automate the optimization of the complex code surrounding language models while preserving the rich diagnostic history needed to improve it?

key_paper.title: Recursive Language Models
key_paper.rationale: This paper introduces an inference strategy that places a long input into an external environment and allows an LLM to inspect it programmatically. We brought this externalized-context idea to harness optimization: instead of compressing previous attempts into a score or summary, we can give the proposer filesystem access to the source code, execution traces, and scores of every prior candidate. We expect this richer interface to preserve long-horizon evidence.

thread.question: Language models can generate and revise executable code using task-level evaluations as feedback. However, code search is difficult because a single score provides little information about which implementation choices caused a behavior or how to change them. How can automated code search use detailed execution evidence to improve complex programs over successive attempts?
thread.criterion: Papers in this thread search over executable programs, using evaluation results to guide successive revisions or select candidates. They provide the foundation for our investigation into how detailed execution evidence can improve automated code search. Work on coding agents qualifies when it develops this search process; general code-generation or software-engineering capabilities alone are insufficient.

samples.title: ScaleCUA: Scaling Open-Source Computer Use Agents with Cross-Platform Data

core_query.question: Recent advances in vision-language models have made it increasingly feasible to automate digital interactions through graphical user interfaces. While proprietary models demonstrate strong capabilities in this domain, progress in open-source computer automation remains fundamentally constrained by the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality training data. Effective computer use requires extensive in-domain knowledge and fine-grained action trajectories, yet such data is costly to collect, highly platform-specific, and vulnerable to becoming outdated as software environments evolve. Although unified, end-to-end agents have shown promise, the limited scale and coverage of existing open-source training corpora continue to restrict their generalization across heterogeneous operating systems and applications. How can we efficiently scale the collection of diverse, high-quality, cross-platform GUI interaction data to train versatile open-source foundation models for autonomous computer use?

key_paper.title: GUIOdyssey: A Comprehensive Dataset for Cross-App GUI Navigation on Mobile Devices
key_paper.rationale: GUIOdyssey introduced a comprehensive cross-app mobile navigation dataset containing 8,334 episodes across 212 applications and 1,357 app combinations, with each step annotated for screen comprehension, historical context, and decision rationale. Its central contribution was to move GUI-agent training beyond short, single-app demonstrations toward long-horizon trajectories that preserve the context required to coordinate actions across applications. Inspired by this work, we incorporated goal-directed, multi-step interaction trajectories and reasoning-oriented supervision into our broader effort to train general-purpose computer-use agents across mobile, desktop, and web environments. We expected this idea to transfer because GUIOdyssey showed that semantic annotations improved performance under both high- and low-level instructions, while its history ablations found that contextual summaries increased overall action-matching accuracy by 9.17 points and success rate by 240% relative to using no historical information.

thread.question: Recent advances in large vision-language models have demonstrated strong multimodal understanding and reasoning capabilities across broad domains. How can we adapt and fine-tune these general-purpose foundational architectures to develop capable agents that autonomously operate graphical user interfaces?
thread.criterion: The positive papers contribute concrete mechanisms for adapting general-purpose vision-language models into GUI agents. Qwen2.5-VL and GPT-4o provide agent-capable visual architectures and GUI-specific vision-language-action training, while GUICourse, UGround, Aria-UI, and the UI-decomposition work introduce scalable grounding and instruction-data formulations. The remaining positive papers contribute complementary methodologies, including task-generalization-based mid-training, trajectory behavior cloning, temporal GUI supervision, and self-evolving environment or reinforcement-learning pipelines. Together, these contributions directly inform backbone selection, data construction, visual grounding, action modeling, and fine-tuning for autonomous GUI operation. In contrast, the GPT-4o System Card and Gemini primarily describe and evaluate broadly capable multimodal foundation models. Although they provide strong baselines and motivate this direction, their primary contributions do not offer a GUI-specific adaptation, training, or interaction methodology.

samples.title: Tensor Product Attention Is All You Need

core_query.question: As language models scale to longer contexts, the memory required for key-value caches and the computational cost of attention during both prefill and autoregressive decoding become major bottlenecks. Existing approaches reduce KV-cache memory through techniques such as sharing or compressing key and value representations, but these savings can come at the cost of representational capacity or computational efficiency. Moreover, some compressed attention mechanisms are tightly coupled to particular positional encoding schemes, making it difficult to combine them cleanly with modern or newly developed positional representations. Can we design an attention representation that simultaneously compresses the KV cache, reduces FLOPs during both prefill and decoding, and remains compatible with arbitrary positional encoding mechanisms?

key_paper.title: DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model
key_paper.rationale: DeepSeek-V2 introduced Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), which compresses the key-value cache into a learned low-dimensional latent representation rather than directly storing independent keys and values for every attention head. This provided strong evidence that learned low-dimensional structure in attention activations could dramatically reduce KV-cache memory while remaining effective in a large-scale language model. The reported reduction in KV-cache size and improvement in generation throughput gave us confidence that activation-level compression, rather than only head sharing, was a viable direction for efficient attention. We took this insight further by asking whether queries, keys, and values could be represented through contextual tensor factorizations, allowing the representation to remain compact while providing greater flexibility across heads and tokens.

thread.question: Modern language models rely on rotary positional embeddings to inject relative positional information by applying rotation matrices to the query and key vectors. How can rotary or other relative positional encoding mechanisms be incorporated into memory- and compute-efficient attention architectures without undermining their efficiency or representational flexibility?
thread.criterion: RoFormer introduced the multiplicative rotary transformations and relative-position property that an efficient compressed attention mechanism must preserve. Linearized Relative Positional Encoding provided a closely related perspective on incorporating positional transformations into attention mechanisms whose query and key representations are structurally factorized, while preserving their computational advantages. Kernelized Attention with Relative Positional Encoding further demonstrated that positional information can be incorporated into a structurally constrained efficient attention formulation without forfeiting its efficiency. The remaining papers either study positional encodings without addressing their interaction with compressed or factorized representations, improve RoPE computation for different objectives, or propose efficient attention mechanisms without addressing how multiplicative positional rotations interact with the compressed representation itself.

samples.title: SPIRAL: Self-Play on Zero-Sum Games Incentivizes Reasoning via Multi-Agent Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning

core_query.question: Recent advances show that applying reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can significantly enhance the reasoning capabilities of large language models, by selecting and reinforcing the generalizable chain-of-thought patterns already latent in pretrained models. However, this approach relies heavily on human curated problem sets and carefully engineered reward functions for specific domains. This manual curation creates a fundamental scalability bottleneck that limits the diversity and volume of reasoning challenges available for training. While competitive self-play has historically driven breakthroughs in other artificial intelligence domains by providing automated feedback and a natural curriculum, applying these dynamics to language models for general problem solving remains largely unexplored. Can language models continue to develop general reasoning through competitive self-play without relying on an ever-growing supply of human-curated problems and hand-engineered rewards?

key_paper.title: Self-playing Adversarial Language Game Enhances LLM Reasoning
key_paper.rationale: It showed that self-play on a single two-player adversarial language game improves an instruction-tuned LLM on general reasoning benchmarks. The gain came from the game alone, with no task-specific reasoning data. The training used offline RL, not an online self-play loop. The authors released the training code. I did not take the central idea from this paper. I reached the same direction on my own, and read the paper afterward. Its contribution still helped me in two concrete ways. First, it was a prior existence proof that the direction was real. Second, its code base gave me a reference point for a self-play setup on a language game. Its own version was limited: one hand-built game, offline RL, instruction-tuned models only, and no online self-play. It did not scale. I redesigned the optimization and the code from scratch. My version runs self-play online, across many games, and on base and reasoning models. The paper reported measurable reasoning gains from self-play on one crude offline game with an instruction-tuned model. This is published evidence, not assumption, that a self-play game signal can raise reasoning. One offline game already produced transfer. So a scalable online version, across many games and on stronger base and reasoning models, was likely to go further.

thread.question: Research on interactive environments suggests that training agents on specific games can cultivate fundamental cognitive patterns that transfer broadly to out of domain cognitive tasks. What types of structured interactive environments can naturally scaffold the development of distinct logical and strategic skills in language models such that these skills generalize to formal academic reasoning domains?
thread.criterion:
This direction asks which structured interactive environments or games cultivate skills in language models that TRANSFER to general, out-of-domain reasoning. A paper is Positive only if its primary contribution supplies a mechanism or substantiated thesis for how training inside a game or environment yields skills that carry OUT of that game to reasoning tasks. Benchmark or measurement-only papers, in-domain agent-improvement with no external transfer, and position or roadmap papers are Negative. "Play to Generalize: Learning to Reason Through Game Play" is the cleanest fit: RL on arcade games produces a 7B multimodal model that improves on MathVista, MMMU, and VSI-Bench without seeing math or diagrams. "Logic-RL: Unleashing LLM Reasoning with Rule-Based Reinforcement Learning" trains on synthetic logic puzzles and shows emergent skills generalizing to AIME and AMC math. "Game-RL: Synthesizing Multimodal Verifiable Game Data to Boost VLMs' General Reasoning" trains VLMs solely on game-derived tasks and reports gains across seven vision-language benchmarks.  "Boundless Socratic Learning with Language Games" is a position paper that envisions endless game learning can drive continuous general capability improvement.

The Negatives fail the transfer bar: "GameBench: Evaluating Strategic Reasoning Abilities of LLM Agents" and "Measuring General Intelligence with Generated Games" are evaluation benchmarks that train nothing. "Situated Language Learning via Interactive Narratives", and "Large Language Models as Agents in Two-Player Games" are position or roadmap papers with no demonstrated out-of-domain transfer mechanism. "Knowledge-enhanced Agents for Interactive Text Games", "EnvGen: Generating and Adapting Environments via LLMs for Training Embodied Agents", and "STARLING: Self-supervised Training of Text-based Reinforcement Learning Agent with Large Language Models" improve agents only within their own game or embodied domain. "ScienceWorld: Is your Agent Smarter than a 5th Grader?" is primarily a benchmark whose evidence stays within the same environment, and "Emergent Communication of Generalizations" concerns compositionality of emergent languages, not transfer to external reasoning.
